why: The pain point is operational overhead and capacity planning. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL is a managed, auto-scaling-storage, PostgreSQL-compatible database, and AWS Fargate with ECS runs the existing containers without managing hosts or cluster capacity. Together they remove infrastructure maintenance from both tiers.

others.B: EC2 instances still require patching, scaling and capacity planning, so overhead is not reduced.
others.C: CloudFront improves content delivery latency but does nothing about managing hosts or the database.
others.D: ElastiCache adds another component to operate and addresses read performance, not operational overhead.

tip: Containers + 'no servers to manage' = Fargate; PostgreSQL + managed + scalable = Aurora.

why: A target tracking scaling policy keeps a metric such as ASGAverageCPUUtilization at a set value (40%) by automatically adding or removing instances. It is purpose-built for 'keep metric at X' requirements and needs no step tuning.

others.A: Simple scaling reacts to alarm thresholds with fixed adjustments and cooldowns, so it does not hold CPU near a target.
others.C: A custom Lambda function reinvents what target tracking already does natively, adding overhead.
others.D: Scheduled scaling is time-based and cannot respond to actual CPU utilization.

tip: 'Keep metric at or near N%' = target tracking policy.

why: An origin access identity (OAI) lets CloudFront authenticate to S3, and a bucket policy granting read only to the OAI blocks direct S3 URL access. Today AWS recommends Origin Access Control (OAC), the successor to OAI, but the principle is the same.

others.A: Policies granting 'CloudFront access' generically are not possible without an OAI/OAC principal, and there is only one bucket.
others.B: CloudFront cannot be assigned an IAM user to sign requests to S3.
others.C: A distribution ID is not a valid principal; OAC uses the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal with a SourceArn condition.

tip: Restrict S3 to CloudFront only = OAI (legacy) or OAC (current).

why: Static downloadable reports fit Amazon S3, which needs no provisioning and scales automatically, and CloudFront caches them at edge locations globally for the fastest response time at low cost.

others.B: Lambda and DynamoDB are for dynamic compute and data, not efficient global delivery of static files.
others.C: EC2 with ALB requires provisioning infrastructure and is regional, so it is costlier and slower globally.
others.D: Internal ALBs are not internet-facing and Route 53 adds no caching.

tip: Global static content, cheap and fast = S3 + CloudFront.

why: RDS Custom for Oracle is a managed database that still grants access to the underlying OS and database host, which standard RDS does not. It supports cross-Region read replicas for DR, minimizing operational overhead compared with self-managed EC2.

others.A: Oracle on EC2 gives OS access but you must manage installation, upgrades and replication yourself, which is high overhead.
others.B: Standard RDS for Oracle does not allow access to the operating system.
others.D: Standard RDS gives no OS access, and a Multi-AZ standby in the same Region is high availability, not Regional DR.

tip: Managed database + OS access needed = RDS Custom (Oracle or SQL Server).

why: Using the existing bucket with Cross-Region Replication, SSE-S3 encryption, and Amazon Athena (serverless SQL directly on S3) gives the least operational overhead. SSE-S3 needs no key management and replicates without extra KMS configuration.

others.A: A new bucket and KMS multi-Region keys add migration and key-management work beyond what is required.
others.B: Amazon RDS is not serverless SQL over S3 data and requires loading data into a database.
others.D: RDS cannot query S3 objects in place and is not a serverless analytics service.

tip: Serverless SQL on S3 = Athena; simplest encryption = SSE-S3.

why: AWS PrivateLink lets the provider expose its service through an endpoint service, and the company creates an interface VPC endpoint to it. Traffic stays private, is limited to that one service, and connections can only be initiated from the consumer VPC.

others.A: VPC peering exposes whole networks bidirectionally rather than restricting access to a single service.
others.B: A virtual private gateway is for VPN or Direct Connect, not private service-specific consumer connectivity.
others.C: A NAT gateway sends traffic to the internet, so it is not private connectivity.

tip: Private, one-way access to a single service in another VPC = PrivateLink.

why: AWS DMS needs a replication instance (server) and a task configured for full load plus ongoing replication (CDC). That keeps Aurora in sync while the on-premises source stays online.

others.B: A backup is a point-in-time copy and cannot keep the target continuously synchronized.
others.D: SCT is unnecessary for a homogeneous PostgreSQL-to-Aurora PostgreSQL migration.
others.E: EventBridge does not monitor or provide database synchronization.

tip: Homogeneous migration needs no SCT; 'stay in sync' = DMS ongoing replication (CDC).

why: Making each root email a distribution list delivers notifications to several administrators, so none is missed, while still limiting recipients to admins. Configuring alternate contacts (billing, operations, security) through Organizations routes specific notifications to the right people.

others.A: Forwarding to all users in the organization violates the requirement to limit notifications to administrators.
others.C: A single administrator is still a single point of failure for missed alerts.
others.D: Each AWS account requires a unique root email address, so they cannot share one.

tip: Root email best practice = distribution list + alternate contacts.

why: Amazon MQ provides managed RabbitMQ with redundant brokers, a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group makes the application tier highly available, and RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ gives managed automatic failover. Every tier becomes highly available with minimal operational overhead.

others.A: Running PostgreSQL in an Auto Scaling group is self-managed and does not handle replication or failover correctly.
others.C: Self-managing RabbitMQ on EC2 adds operational overhead compared with Amazon MQ.
others.D: Self-managing both the queue and the database on EC2 maximizes operational overhead.

tip: RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ lift-and-shift = Amazon MQ.

why: S3 replication copies new objects automatically without custom code. Sending the analysis bucket's events to Amazon EventBridge allows a rule to target multiple consumers, including Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines, which plain S3 event notifications cannot target.

others.A: A custom copy Lambda adds code to maintain, and S3 event notifications cannot target SageMaker Pipelines.
others.B: A custom copy Lambda adds overhead compared with native S3 replication.
others.C: S3 event notifications support only SNS, SQS and Lambda as destinations, not SageMaker Pipelines.

tip: S3 events to many targets or non-Lambda/SQS/SNS targets = EventBridge.

why: Interruptible, sporadic EC2 workloads are ideal for Spot Instances, which offer the deepest discount. A Compute Savings Plan is the only Savings Plan that covers Fargate and Lambda, and it fits predictable one-year usage.

others.B: On-Demand is far more expensive than Spot for interruptible work.
others.D: Reserved Instances suit steady usage, not sporadic, unpredictable workloads.
others.E: EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply only to EC2, not Fargate or Lambda.

tip: Fargate or Lambda discounts = Compute Savings Plan.

why: CloudFront accelerates both static and dynamic content. It caches static objects at the edge, and for dynamic requests it uses the AWS backbone, persistent connections and TLS termination near users, with the ALB as origin. This gives the lowest latency globally from a single Region stack.

others.B: This option has no text in the source and is not a valid solution.
others.C: Serving dynamic content straight from the ALB forgoes CloudFront's edge network optimizations for distant users.
others.D: Two Regions still leave many users far from an origin and add no edge caching or acceleration.

tip: CloudFront is not only for static content; it accelerates dynamic content too.

why: AWS Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IP addresses, routes UDP or TCP traffic to the nearest edge location, and carries it over the AWS backbone. A Network Load Balancer supports UDP, and EC2 instances can run a modified Linux kernel.

others.A: ALB supports only HTTP/HTTPS, and Lambda cannot run a custom kernel.
others.B: CloudFront does not support arbitrary UDP traffic and has no static IPs, and Lambda cannot run a custom kernel.
others.D: API Gateway and ALB handle HTTP only, not UDP, and API Gateway has no static IPs.

tip: UDP + static IPs + edge routing = Global Accelerator + NLB.

why: Containerizing each smaller application on Amazon ECS keeps most of the existing code, lets each team own a separate service, and scales well. An ALB with path-based routing fronts the services, so this is the least-overhead microservices approach.

others.A: Lambda would require substantial rewriting of the monolith into functions.
others.B: Amplify with Lambda also requires rewriting the backend into serverless functions.
others.C: EC2 Auto Scaling groups do not easily separate the app into independently managed services and carry more host overhead.

tip: Break up a monolith while keeping code = containers on ECS or EKS.

why: Pointing the reporting workload at an Aurora Replica offloads the read-heavy queries from the writer instance using the shared storage volume. It needs no new service and is cheaper than scaling up or moving to Redshift.

others.A: Redshift adds a separate data warehouse and ETL pipeline, which costs more than a replica for monthly reports.
others.C: A larger instance runs at higher cost 24/7 to handle a monthly spike.
others.D: Aurora does not use Provisioned IOPS in the same way, and IOPS would not fix CPU contention.

tip: Reporting load slowing the primary = read replica.

why: Moving MySQL to Aurora separates the database tier, and an Auto Scaling group built from a launch template scales the web tier seamlessly behind an ALB. Using Spot capacity makes the scaling tier the most cost-effective option, since the web tier is stateless once the database is moved off.

others.A: A fixed second On-Demand instance does not scale seamlessly and costs more than Spot.
others.B: Route 53 weighted routing with two fixed instances provides no automatic scaling or health-based load balancing.
others.C: Stopping the instance to resize it causes downtime and is vertical scaling, not seamless scaling.

tip: 'Scale seamlessly' = Auto Scaling group + load balancer; 'most cost-effective' often signals Spot.

why: The steady baseline running around the clock suits Reserved Instances (or Savings Plans) for the biggest committed discount. The extra daytime peak capacity can use Spot Instances, and because the app is stateless behind an ALB, interruptions are tolerated without affecting availability.

others.A: An all-Spot fleet risks losing baseline capacity when instances are reclaimed, harming availability.
others.C: On-Demand for the always-on baseline is more expensive than Reserved Instances.
others.D: Dedicated Instances cost more and are not needed, and On-Demand for peaks is pricier than Spot.

tip: Baseline = RIs or Savings Plans; spiky stateless extra = Spot.

why: Amazon S3 stores the logs cheaply, and an S3 Lifecycle rule automatically transitions objects older than 30 days to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest class for rarely accessed 10-year retention. Lifecycle rules are native and cost nothing extra to configure.

others.A: AWS Backup does not transition S3 objects between storage classes; that is the job of Lifecycle policies.
others.C: CloudWatch Logs storage for over 10 TB per month is expensive, and AWS Backup cannot move it to Deep Archive.
others.D: S3 Lifecycle policies cannot act on CloudWatch Logs data.

tip: Age-based storage class transitions = S3 Lifecycle.

why: With asynchronous invocation from SNS, Lambda can send events that fail after its retries to an on-failure destination such as an SQS queue. The function (or a retry consumer) can then process the queued messages later, so every notification is eventually processed instead of being lost.

others.A: Lambda already runs across multiple AZs, and that does not fix transient network failures.
others.B: More CPU or memory does not address network connectivity failures.
others.C: SNS retry policies apply to delivery to the endpoint, not to failures inside the function's processing, and retries eventually run out.

tip: Never lose failed async events = SQS DLQ or on-failure destination.

why: An SQS FIFO queue preserves strict message order (within a message group) and offers exactly-once processing. Lambda can poll it natively, so the setup is fully managed with minimal operational overhead.

others.B: Standard SNS topics do not guarantee ordering.
others.C: SQS standard queues provide only best-effort ordering.
others.D: A standard SNS topic and queue do not guarantee order, and no processing compute is defined.

tip: Ordering required = FIFO (SQS FIFO or SNS FIFO).

why: CloudWatch composite alarms combine multiple alarms with AND/OR logic, so an alarm fires only when high CPU and high read IOPS occur together. That reduces false alarms from short CPU bursts.

others.B: Dashboards only visualize data and require humans to watch, so they cannot alert automatically.
others.C: Synthetics canaries test endpoints and user flows, not combined infrastructure metric conditions.
others.D: A single metric alarm evaluates one metric (or one math expression) and is not the intended way to require two independent alarm states.

tip: Alarm only when X AND Y = composite alarm.

why: AWS Control Tower offers preventive guardrails (controls), including Region deny and controls that disallow internet access. Organizations SCPs can also deny actions such as creating internet gateways and deny all Regions except ap-northeast-3 across accounts. Both prevent the action instead of just detecting it.

others.B: AWS WAF filters HTTP requests and cannot block VPC internet connectivity, and there is no account setting that denies Regions.
others.D: NACLs can be changed by administrators, and per-user IAM policies are hard to maintain and easy to bypass compared with SCPs.
others.E: AWS Config is detective only; it alerts after the fact rather than preventing the action.

tip: Prevent across accounts = SCPs or Control Tower preventive controls; Config = detect.

why: Scheduled EventBridge rules invoking Lambda functions that call StartDBInstance and StopDBInstance stop the RDS instance during the 12 unused hours, cutting instance-hour costs with serverless, near-zero-cost automation.

others.A: Session Manager provides shell access to instances and has nothing to do with scheduling RDS start or stop.
others.B: Adding ElastiCache increases cost, and serving data while the DB is stopped is not required.
others.C: A dedicated EC2 instance running cron adds cost and management overhead compared with Lambda.

tip: Scheduled start or stop = EventBridge Scheduler or rule + Lambda (or Instance Scheduler).

why: Access patterns are known (rarely downloaded after 90 days), so a simple S3 Lifecycle rule moving objects to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days is the cheapest option. The files are at least 128 KB, so the Standard-IA minimum billable size is not a penalty, and recent files stay in Standard.

others.A: Storing new popular files in Standard-IA incurs retrieval fees on frequent access.
others.B: Intelligent-Tiering adds a per-object monitoring fee across millions of objects and does not let you set a 90-day rule; it is best for unknown patterns.
others.C: S3 Inventory reports on objects and cannot transition them.

tip: Known access pattern = Lifecycle; unknown = Intelligent-Tiering.

why: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode makes objects WORM: no user, including root, can overwrite or delete a version until the retention period (365 days) ends. IAM permissions then control who can add files and who has read-only access.

others.A: Governance mode can be bypassed by users with special permissions, and a legal hold has no fixed period.
others.C: IAM policies can be changed by administrators, so they do not guarantee immutability.
others.D: Hash tracking only detects modifications after they happen; it does not prevent them.

tip: Nobody can delete, not even root = Object Lock compliance mode.

why: Amazon CloudFront caches S3 content at edge locations worldwide for fast, reliable delivery regardless of user location. Confidential files can be protected with OAC plus signed URLs or signed cookies.

others.A: DataSync is a data transfer and migration service, not a content delivery or caching layer.
others.B: Global Accelerator does not cache content and does not support S3 buckets as endpoints.
others.D: SQS is a message queue and cannot deliver or cache files.

tip: Caching content globally = CloudFront.

why: Lake Formation blueprints with AWS Glue crawlers and ETL ingest batch database data into an S3 data lake as Parquet with little custom code. Athena then runs serverless one-time SQL queries on S3, and QuickSight builds KPI dashboards, all fully managed.

others.B: Kinesis Data Analytics is for continuous streaming analytics, not ad hoc one-time queries.
others.C: Custom record-by-record Lambda functions into Redshift add significant development and operational overhead.
others.D: Running multiple OpenSearch clusters is costly to operate and not the stated S3 staging approach.

tip: Data lake on S3 = Lake Formation + Glue; ad hoc SQL = Athena; BI = QuickSight.

why: Aurora automated backups max out at 35 days, so AWS Backup with a 5-year retention rule (and automatic deletion) meets the data requirement. Exporting the Aurora PostgreSQL audit or database logs to CloudWatch Logs with never-expire retention keeps audit logs indefinitely.

others.A: A manual snapshot is a single point in time, never expires automatically, and does not delete data after 5 years.
others.B: Aurora automated backups do not support lifecycle policies.
others.C: Automated backup retention is limited to 35 days.

tip: RDS or Aurora backups beyond 35 days = AWS Backup or manual snapshots.

why: CloudFront delivers both live streaming (for example HLS or DASH segments from MediaPackage or MediaLive) and on-demand video from edge locations close to the global audience, improving performance for both.

others.B: Global Accelerator improves TCP/UDP routing but does not cache video segments at the edge.
others.C: Route 53 is DNS and does not accelerate or cache content.
others.D: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads into S3, not streaming to viewers.

tip: Live or VOD streaming to a global audience = CloudFront.

why: AWS WAF attached to API Gateway can block bot traffic using rate-based rules, IP reputation lists and Bot Control. A usage plan with API keys issued only to genuine users adds throttling and quota control to identify legitimate clients.

others.B: Filtering in Lambda still incurs invocations and costs, and maintaining IP lists in code is fragile.
others.D: A private API is reachable only from within VPCs, which would cut off legitimate public users.
others.E: Creating an IAM role per public user does not scale and is impractical.

tip: Block bots or malicious requests on API Gateway or ALB or CloudFront = AWS WAF.

why: Only about 300 MB per month for 30 days is tiny, and S3 Standard offers millisecond access with no retrieval fees or minimum duration penalties. That makes it the most cost-effective option for this backup.

others.A: OpenSearch Service requires running a cluster, which is far costlier for simple backup storage.
others.B: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours to retrieve, and its 90-day minimum exceeds the 30-day need.
others.D: Running an RDS instance to hold JSON backups is costly and unnecessary.

tip: Millisecond access + short retention + small data = S3 Standard.

why: S3 event notifications invoking Lambda process each JSON document as it arrives, with automatic scaling and built-in high availability and no servers to manage. Aurora provides a managed, highly available SQL database for the results.

others.A: Running EC2 instances requires managing scaling, patching and availability.
others.C: EBS Multi-Attach works only with io1/io2 in a single AZ and needs a cluster-aware file system, so it is not highly available.
others.D: ECS on the EC2 launch type still requires managing cluster instances, and SQS message size limits suit references rather than documents.

tip: Process files as they land in S3 = S3 event + Lambda.

why: Amazon FSx for Lustre is a high-performance parallel file system for Linux HPC. It natively links to an S3 bucket via a data repository association, lazy-loading datasets and exporting outputs back to S3 for durable long-term storage.

others.B: FSx for Windows File Server targets Windows SMB workloads, not Linux HPC, and has no native S3 linking.
others.C: Glacier is archival with slow retrieval and is not a file system for active processing.
others.D: An EBS gp2 volume is block storage attached to one instance and cannot be shared by hundreds of instances.

tip: HPC + Linux + S3 integration = FSx for Lustre.

why: ECR stores the images, and ECS on AWS Fargate runs containers without any EC2 hosts to manage. Tasks are spread across AZs for high availability, and target tracking Service Auto Scaling handles demand. This minimizes operational overhead for a team new to container orchestration.

others.B: The EC2 launch type requires managing, patching and scaling the container instances.
others.C: Self-hosting a registry and manually launching instances is high operational overhead.
others.D: Baking containers into AMIs abandons container orchestration and requires managing instances.

tip: Containers + least overhead = ECS (or EKS) on Fargate.

why: SQS decouples the applications, retains messages up to 14 days (well above the 2-day processing window), and scales easily for about 1,000 messages per hour. A dead-letter queue isolates messages that repeatedly fail so they do not block the rest, all fully managed.

others.A: A self-managed Redis on EC2 adds operational burden and is not a durable queue.
others.B: Kinesis is for high-throughput ordered streaming and has no built-in per-message dead-letter handling.
others.D: SNS is push-based with no message retention for long processing or failed-message isolation.

tip: Decouple + retain failures = SQS + DLQ.

why: AWS WAF is associated directly with the CloudFront distribution, so every viewer request is inspected. An OAI (now OAC) restricts the S3 bucket so it can be reached only through CloudFront, preventing anyone from bypassing WAF via the S3 URL.

others.A: S3 bucket policies cannot reference a WAF ARN as a principal.
others.B: CloudFront does not forward requests to WAF; WAF is attached to the distribution as a web ACL.
others.C: Security groups cannot be applied to S3 buckets.

tip: WAF on CloudFront + OAC so the origin cannot be bypassed.

why: CloudFront with the S3 bucket as origin caches the static HTML at edge locations worldwide. It handles millions of views with low latency and reduces S3 request costs.

others.A: Presigned URLs grant temporary access to private objects but do nothing for global performance.
others.B: Replicating to every Region is costly and complex and still lacks edge caching.
others.C: Route 53 geoproximity routing needs multiple endpoints and provides no caching.

tip: Static content, global audience = CloudFront + S3.

why: Reserved Instances cover the steady baseline at a discount, while On-Demand Instances handle unpredictable extra capacity without interruption risk. This meets the 'continually process without downtime' requirement.

others.A: Spot-only capacity can be reclaimed at any time, risking downtime.
others.B: Reserving for maximum capacity wastes money during intermittent low traffic.
others.C: Spot for additional capacity is cheaper but can be interrupted, and the keyed answer prioritizes no downtime.

tip: Interruption must be avoided = On-Demand rather than Spot for burst capacity.
flag: SQS consumers are idempotent-friendly and interruptions just return messages to the queue, so many argue C (RIs + Spot) is more cost-effective without real downtime.

why: A service control policy attached to the root OU applies to every account in the organization. It sets maximum permissions centrally, so denying specific services or actions there is scalable and maintained in one place.

others.A: Network ACLs control subnet traffic, not access to AWS services or API actions.
others.B: Security groups control network traffic to resources and cannot be attached to users or accounts.
others.C: Roles in each account are not a single point of maintenance and do not inherently restrict other principals.

tip: Restrict all accounts centrally = SCP.

why: AWS Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation for ALBs, CloudFront, Route 53 and Global Accelerator. It adds 24/7 Shield Response Team support, cost protection and automatic application-layer mitigation with WAF.

others.A: Amazon Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and cannot be installed on an ALB or mitigate DDoS.
others.B: This option text is an artifact of the source data and is not a valid solution.
others.D: GuardDuty detects threats from logs but does not mitigate DDoS attacks.

tip: DDoS protection = Shield (Standard free, Advanced for enhanced).

why: The intended answer is an AWS WAF web ACL on the ALB with a geographic match rule that allows only the specific country and blocks the rest. WAF can inspect request origin by country, which network controls cannot.

others.A: Security groups filter by IP or CIDR and port and have no country-based filtering.
others.B: ALB security groups also cannot filter by country.
others.D: Network ACLs filter IP ranges only and cannot practically enforce country restrictions.

tip: Allow or block by country = WAF geo match (or CloudFront geo restriction). Option C text is missing in the source; it should be AWS WAF on the ALB.

why: API Gateway with Lambda is serverless and scales automatically and elastically with the holiday spike. Capacity drops back when demand falls, and no instances need to be provisioned.

others.A: A single EC2 instance does not scale elastically and is a single point of failure.
others.C: Two fixed EC2 instances behind an ALB have no automatic scaling.
others.D: API Gateway in front of a single EC2 instance still bottlenecks on that instance.

tip: Elastic and scalable API with least management = API Gateway + Lambda.

why: CloudFront field-level encryption encrypts specific sensitive POST fields at the edge with a public key. The data stays encrypted through the whole stack and only applications holding the private key can decrypt it, on top of HTTPS.

others.A: Signed URLs control who can access content, not protection of submitted data fields.
others.B: Signed cookies also control access to content and do not encrypt user-submitted data.
others.D: HTTPS-only protects data in transit between hops but not throughout the stack, and it is already in use.

tip: Protect specific sensitive form fields end to end = CloudFront field-level encryption.

why: CloudFront caches the identical media files at edge locations globally, serving millions of users while greatly reducing origin requests. It is cost-effective because CloudFront data transfer out is often cheaper than direct S3 transfer.

others.A: Global Accelerator does not cache content, so origin load is not reduced.
others.C: ElastiCache for Redis is an in-memory cache for application data, not for global delivery of large media files.
others.D: Memcached has the same limitation and does not serve users at the edge.

tip: Reduce origin load for static media worldwide = CloudFront.

why: Spreading the existing Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones (three instances in each) behind the same ALB survives an AZ failure. No application change is needed because ALB and Auto Scaling are natively multi-AZ.

others.A: An Auto Scaling group cannot span Regions, and multi-Region requires more redesign.
others.C: A template for manual launches in another Region is not automatic high availability.
others.D: Changing the routing algorithm does not remove the single-AZ point of failure.

tip: High availability within a Region = Multi-AZ.

why: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, so a surge of Lambda invocations does not exhaust Aurora connections, CPU and memory. The only code change is pointing the function at the proxy endpoint.

others.A: Provisioned concurrency would create more connections, and a global database does not fix connection exhaustion.
others.C: Order processing involves writes, so a read replica does not help, and query-string routing requires application changes.
others.D: Migrating to DynamoDB is a major application rewrite.

tip: Lambda + RDS or Aurora 'too many connections' = RDS Proxy.

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB keeps traffic on the AWS network without internet or NAT access. Endpoint policies can restrict which tables are reachable, making it the most secure option at no extra cost.

others.B: A NAT gateway routes traffic toward the public DynamoDB endpoint and costs extra, so it is less secure.
others.C: This option text is an artifact of the source data and is not a valid solution.
others.D: An internet gateway requires public routing, so traffic leaves the private network path.

tip: S3 and DynamoDB private access = gateway endpoint (free).

why: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, API-compatible in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond reads. The application keeps using DynamoDB API calls with minimal change and no cache logic to write.

others.A: ElastiCache for Redis requires application code to implement caching logic.
others.C: Global tables replicate across Regions for multi-Region availability, not read caching.
others.D: Memcached also requires application changes to manage the cache.

tip: Speed up DynamoDB reads without code changes = DAX.

why: AWS Backup centrally manages backups for both EC2 and RDS. A backup plan with a cross-Region copy rule automatically copies recovery points to another Region, giving the least operational overhead.

others.B: Data Lifecycle Manager handles EBS snapshots and AMIs but not RDS backups.
others.C: Manual AMI copying and running a read replica add effort and ongoing cost.
others.D: A multi-step snapshot, export and replication process has high operational overhead.

tip: Centralized, cross-Region backup for many services = AWS Backup.

why: An IAM role attached to the EC2 instance (via an instance profile) supplies temporary credentials. The role needs ssm:GetParameter on the SecureString parameter and kms:Decrypt on the KMS key that encrypts it.

others.B: IAM policies cannot be attached directly to an EC2 instance; they must go through a role and instance profile.
others.C: Parameters are not principals for trust relationships, and RDS is not the caller.
others.D: A trust relationship between a DB instance and EC2 is not an IAM concept and grants no Parameter Store access.

tip: EC2 accessing AWS APIs = IAM role (instance profile), never keys.

why: AWS WAF on API Gateway blocks SQL injection and other web exploits at the API entry point. The intended option B is AWS Shield Advanced with the NLB, which adds detection and mitigation of large, sophisticated DDoS attacks plus Shield Response Team support.

others.A: AWS WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer.
others.D: GuardDuty is threat detection and Shield Standard offers only basic DDoS protection without advanced mitigation.
others.E: Shield Standard is automatic and free but lacks advanced DDoS detection and mitigation.

tip: Web exploits = WAF; large sophisticated DDoS = Shield Advanced. Option B text is missing in the source; it should be Shield Advanced with the NLB.

why: An SQS queue decouples producers and consumers among microservices. Each message is processed by one consumer, consumers can scale horizontally on ECS, and ordering is not required, so a standard queue fits.

others.B: SNS fans out to every subscriber and does not buffer work for consumers to pull at their own pace.
others.C: A Lambda function used as a message relay is not a messaging service, offers no buffering, and couples the services.
others.D: DynamoDB Streams retain data only 24 hours and is a workaround, not a purpose-built work queue.

tip: Decouple producers and consumers, order not needed = SQS standard.

why: RDS MySQL Multi-AZ synchronously replicates every transaction to a standby in another AZ before acknowledging the commit, so each transaction exists on at least two nodes. Failover is automatic, which minimizes data loss.

others.A: Standard RDS does not offer synchronous replication to three nodes, and no engine is specified.
others.C: Read replicas use asynchronous replication.
others.D: A custom Lambda replication scheme is unreliable, complex and not truly synchronous.

tip: Synchronous replication = Multi-AZ; read replicas = asynchronous.

why: S3, CloudFront, API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB are all serverless, so there is no patching. DynamoDB on-demand capacity instantly scales both reads and writes, whereas Aurora Auto Scaling only adds read replicas.

others.B: Aurora Auto Scaling adds Aurora Replicas, which scale reads only, and replicas take minutes to add.
others.C: EC2 requires patching, and provisioned write capacity does not scale as quickly as on-demand.
others.D: EC2 requires server maintenance, and Aurora Auto Scaling does not scale write capacity.

tip: Scale both reads and writes instantly, serverless = DynamoDB on-demand.

why: A console-created Lambda function runs in the AWS-managed network with no route to on premises. Attaching it to the VPC (private subnets plus a security group) gives it ENIs in subnets whose routes already send traffic through the virtual private gateway and Direct Connect.

others.B: Direct Connect already provides connectivity, and the function cannot use it until it is attached to the VPC.
others.C: Route tables do not affect a Lambda function that is not attached to the VPC.
others.D: Lambda cannot be assigned an Elastic IP, and public IPs would not reach a private data center.

tip: Lambda reaching private resources (VPC or on premises) = configure Lambda VPC access.

why: ECS task IAM roles (taskRoleArn in the task definition) provide temporary credentials to the containers in that task. This grants least-privilege S3 access to just that application.

others.A: There is no generic 'S3 role' to update, and the role must be attached to the task.
others.C: Security groups control network traffic, not IAM authorization to S3 APIs, and launch configurations are deprecated.
others.D: IAM users with long-term credentials are not how ECS tasks are authorized.

tip: Container permissions = task role (taskRoleArn); the execution role is for pulling images and logs.

why: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides a fully managed native SMB file share with Active Directory integration. It supports Multi-AZ deployment, so many Windows instances across AZs can share it.

others.A: Volume gateway presents iSCSI block volumes for on-premises backup, not a shared multi-instance file system.
others.C: Amazon EFS uses NFS and is not supported on Windows instances.
others.D: EBS volumes are AZ-scoped, and Multi-Attach does not provide a shared Windows file system across AZs.

tip: Shared Windows SMB storage = FSx for Windows File Server; Linux NFS = EFS.

why: RDS Multi-AZ gives automatic failover for the relational database without manual action. ECS on Fargate runs the containers across AZs without managing servers, so both tiers need minimal manual intervention.

others.B: Read replicas need manual promotion and are not an automatic HA mechanism.
others.C: A self-managed Docker cluster on EC2 needs significant manual operation.
others.E: The EC2 launch type requires managing container instances, so it is more manual than Fargate.

tip: HA database = Multi-AZ; least-management containers = Fargate.

why: AWS Transfer Family provides a fully managed, highly available SFTP endpoint that writes directly to an S3 bucket. There are no servers, scripts or load balancers to run.

others.B: Cron scripts on EC2 instances add operational overhead and delay, and this option is only part of a self-managed design.
others.C: An NLB in front of self-managed SFTP servers still requires managing the EC2 fleet.
others.D: Self-managed SFTP on EC2 in a private subnet is high overhead and is not reachable by the partner.

tip: SFTP, FTPS or FTP into S3 or EFS = AWS Transfer Family.

why: Object Lock in compliance mode prevents any overwrite or delete during the 5-year retention, even by root. SSE-KMS with a customer managed key supports automatic annual key rotation, which you can enable and control.

others.A: Governance mode can be bypassed by users with special permissions, so it does not guarantee immutability.
others.C: SSE-S3 keys are managed and rotated by AWS, and you cannot configure or audit a rotation schedule.
others.E: Imported key material cannot be rotated automatically; rotation must be done manually.

tip: Automatic yearly rotation you control = KMS customer managed key.

why: Elastic Beanstalk is a managed platform for Java and PHP that handles provisioning, load balancing, Auto Scaling and Multi-AZ. Swapping environment URLs (CNAME swap) enables blue/green testing of new features with minimal operational overhead.

others.A: S3 static hosting plus Lambda requires rewriting the Java and PHP app.
others.C: Self-managed EC2 with Auto Scaling and an ALB involves more operational work and has no built-in feature-testing workflow.
others.D: The AWS Load Balancer Controller is for Kubernetes (EKS), and containerizing adds work.

tip: Managed web app platform with blue/green = Elastic Beanstalk URL swap.

why: A read replica offloads the long-running reporting queries from the primary, so order writes no longer time out while employees can still query current data at any time.

others.B: Ordering is write-heavy, and writes cannot go to a read replica.
others.C: Migrating to DynamoDB is a major rewrite and does not suit ad hoc SQL reporting.
others.D: Scheduling reports for off-peak hours prevents employees from running queries when they need them.

tip: Separate reporting from OLTP = read replica.

why: Lambda triggered on upload uses Amazon Textract to extract text from scanned documents and Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify medical entities. The results go to S3 and Athena runs serverless SQL over them, making the solution scalable and operationally efficient.

others.A: MySQL on a single EC2 instance is not scalable and requires management.
others.C: A custom extraction app on EC2 Auto Scaling adds development and operations effort.
others.D: Rekognition targets images and video rather than document text, and Transcribe Medical converts speech, not text.

tip: Text from scans = Textract; medical entities = Comprehend Medical; audio = Transcribe.

why: The keyed answer adds RDS read replicas, which absorb read traffic away from the primary databases and can be promoted, supporting availability. This reduces the read load on each primary without application caching logic.

others.B: ElastiCache for Redis would cache results but requires application changes to implement caching (the keyed answer prefers replicas).
others.C: Route 53 DNS caching caches name resolution, not database query results.
others.D: Memcached has no replication or failover, so it does not ensure high availability.

tip: 'Reduce reads on the DB' often hints at caching; 'scale reads' hints at replicas.
flag: Read replicas spread reads rather than reduce them; ElastiCache for Redis (B) with Multi-AZ replication actually reduces database reads while staying highly available, so B is arguably correct (41% community vote).

why: Two EC2 database instances in different AZs within one Region, configured as a cluster with replication, can fail over automatically to the surviving node during an AZ disruption. That gives high availability on EC2.

others.B: Re-provisioning from an AMI with CloudFormation is backup and restore, not automatic failover, and loses data.
others.C: Cross-Region replication adds latency and complexity and is DR rather than automatic HA.
others.D: EC2 auto recovery handles only underlying host failures in the same AZ and does not protect against AZ events.

tip: HA = multi-AZ within a Region; DR = multi-Region.

why: Placing an SQS queue between the order system and the EC2 workers (in an Auto Scaling group) makes orders durable. If instances fail, messages remain in the queue and are processed automatically after the visibility timeout or by replacement instances.

others.A: An EventBridge rule targeting ECS does not buffer orders or link to the existing processing.
others.B: An ALB distributes requests but does not persist them, so in-flight orders are lost when instances fail.
others.D: SNS, Lambda and Run Command is convoluted and has no durable buffering or retries for the EC2 processing.

tip: Do not lose work during outages = queue (SQS) between tiers.

why: DynamoDB Time to Live automatically deletes items after the epoch timestamp in a designated attribute at no extra cost (TTL deletes consume no write capacity). The only development effort is adding a timestamp of now plus 30 days to new items.

others.A: Redeploying stacks would destroy the table and all data, which is disruptive and wrong.
others.B: A Marketplace monitoring app on EC2 with scripts adds cost and maintenance.
others.C: Lambda deletion logic consumes write capacity and invocation costs and requires custom code.

tip: Auto-expire DynamoDB items = TTL.

why: Rehosting the .NET app on Elastic Beanstalk's Windows .NET platform across multiple AZs requires minimal code change and is highly available. Migrating Oracle to RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ with DMS keeps the same engine and provides automatic failover.

others.A: Refactoring to Lambda requires significant development changes.
others.C: A .NET Framework app built for Windows Server would need porting to run on Amazon Linux.
others.D: Moving from Oracle to DynamoDB requires a major data model and code rewrite.

tip: Minimize changes = keep the same engine and platform (rehost or replatform).

why: Amazon EKS runs the existing Kubernetes manifests and deployment methods unchanged, and Fargate removes worker-node management. Amazon DocumentDB is MongoDB-compatible, so the application code does not change and operational overhead is minimal.

others.A: ECS changes the deployment method away from Kubernetes, and MongoDB on EC2 is self-managed.
others.B: ECS changes the deployment method, and DynamoDB would require code changes.
others.C: DynamoDB is not MongoDB-compatible, and EC2 worker nodes add management overhead.

tip: Kubernetes = EKS; MongoDB = DocumentDB.

why: Amazon Transcribe converts call audio to text and supports speaker diarization (identifying multiple speakers). The transcripts are stored in S3, where Athena can query them with SQL, and S3 retention or Lifecycle rules keep them for 7 years.

others.A: Rekognition analyzes images and video, not speech, so it cannot recognize speakers in audio.
others.C: Translate converts text between languages and does not recognize speakers or transcribe audio.
others.D: Rekognition cannot transcribe audio, and Textract extracts text from documents rather than analyzing transcripts.

tip: Speech to text with speaker labels = Transcribe.

why: API Gateway has a built-in Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer that validates the users' JWT tokens on each request. It is AWS managed and needs no custom code, so it has the least operational overhead.

others.A: A Lambda authorizer requires writing and maintaining custom validation code.
others.B: API keys are for usage plans and metering, not user authentication, and Lambda validation adds code.
others.C: Trusting an email header is insecure and requires custom Lambda logic.

tip: Cognito users + API Gateway = Cognito user pool authorizer.

why: Amazon Pinpoint (now AWS End User Messaging for SMS) supports two-way SMS, so users can reply. Journeys handle the messaging, and event streaming to Kinesis lets responses be archived and analyzed for a year.

others.A: Amazon Connect is a contact center service, not the right tool for marketing SMS campaigns with stored responses.
others.C: SQS is a message queue and cannot send SMS to phones.
others.D: SNS FIFO topics do not deliver SMS, and SNS SMS does not natively capture two-way replies for analysis.

tip: Two-way SMS or marketing campaigns = Pinpoint or End User Messaging.

why: The keyed answer relies on SSE-S3, which encrypts all objects at rest with AWS managed keys that AWS rotates automatically. It needs no key creation or configuration, so it has the least operational overhead.

others.B: A KMS customer managed key with automatic rotation works but adds key management and KMS request costs.
others.C: Manual rotation adds operational overhead.
others.D: Imported key material cannot be rotated automatically and requires client-side encryption effort.

tip: SSE-S3 = zero management; KMS CMK = you control and audit rotation.
flag: AWS does not document a guaranteed yearly rotation for SSE-S3 keys, whereas a KMS customer managed key with automatic rotation verifiably rotates yearly, so B arguably meets the explicit requirement better.

why: The bottleneck is the invitation-sending consumers falling behind on the SQS queue. An Auto Scaling group that scales on queue depth (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible or backlog per instance) adds consumers as messages pile up, cutting delivery delay.

others.A: DAX speeds DynamoDB reads, but the delay is in processing the queue, not database reads.
others.B: API Gateway in front of the intake app does not speed up downstream processing.
others.C: CloudFront caching does not help the queue-consuming application process messages faster.

tip: SQS consumers lagging = scale workers on queue depth.

why: AWS Lake Formation builds a governed data lake over S3 and, via a Glue JDBC connection, the RDS data. It provides centralized fine-grained (database, table, column and row level) permissions for many teams with minimal operational overhead.

others.A: Moving purchase data into RDS does not scale for analytics and RDS access controls are coarse for analysts.
others.B: S3 bucket policies cannot provide table- or column-level permissions, and custom copy Lambdas add overhead.
others.D: A Redshift cluster with custom copy jobs adds cost and operational overhead.

tip: Fine-grained permissions on a data lake = Lake Formation.

why: A private S3 bucket serving as the CloudFront origin, accessible only through an OAI (now OAC), is the cheapest and most resilient way to host static documents. S3 is durable and serverless, and infrequent updates via the AWS CLI cost nothing extra.

others.A: A single Lightsail instance is a single point of failure.
others.B: An EC2 Auto Scaling group and ALB are costly overkill for static content.
others.D: Transfer Family SFTP endpoints carry an hourly charge, and a public bucket is less secure.

tip: Static site behind CloudFront = private S3 + OAC.

why: EventBridge receives CloudTrail-recorded management events such as ec2:CreateImage in near real time. A rule matching that API call can target an SNS topic for alerts with no code, which is the least operational overhead.

others.A: A custom Lambda function polling CloudTrail logs adds code and delay.
others.B: Querying with Athena after log delivery is slow and needs manual or scheduled queries.
others.D: CloudTrail cannot target SQS directly, and custom Lambda logic adds overhead.

tip: React to a specific API call = EventBridge rule on CloudTrail events.

why: An SQS queue buffers incoming requests so bursts do not exceed DynamoDB's provisioned throughput. Lambda then writes from the queue at a controlled rate, so requests are no longer lost and users are not throttled or affected.

others.A: API Gateway throttling rejects requests, which affects existing users.
others.B: This option has no text in the source and is not a valid solution.
others.C: A secondary index increases write consumption and does not add write capacity.

tip: Protect a throughput-limited backend from spikes = SQS buffer.

why: An interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) for S3 keeps API calls and data on private IPs within AWS. A bucket policy allowing only the EC2 instance's IAM role, optionally with an aws:SourceVpce condition, restricts upload access to that instance.

others.B: Gateway endpoints attach to route tables at the VPC level (not per AZ) and do not support security groups, so the option is technically wrong as written.
others.C: S3 endpoint IPs are public and change, and static routes do not provide private routing.
others.D: ip-ranges.json lists public IP ranges, and routing to them still traverses public routes.

tip: Gateway endpoint = route table, no SGs; interface endpoint = ENI with SGs.

why: With instances scaling in and out frequently, session state must live outside the instances. Amazon ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) provides a fast, shared, distributed session store that every instance can read.

others.B: Sticky sessions lose session data when an instance terminates during scale-in and are not distributed.
others.C: Systems Manager Session Manager provides shell access to instances, not application session storage.
others.D: STS GetSessionToken issues temporary AWS credentials and does not manage application sessions.

tip: Distributed session state = ElastiCache (or DynamoDB).

why: SQS queues decouple order collection from fulfillment so data is not lost during scaling. Scaling each Auto Scaling group on a custom backlog-per-instance metric (queue depth divided by running instances) with target tracking matches capacity to the work and optimizes resource use.

others.A: Setting minimum capacity to peak values wastes resources off-peak.
others.B: Creating additional Auto Scaling groups on demand via SNS is not how scaling works, and CPU does not reflect queue backlog.
others.C: SQS does not send scaling notifications; scaling must be driven by CloudWatch metrics.

tip: AWS-recommended SQS scaling = backlog-per-instance target tracking.

why: The AWS Resource Groups Tag Editor searches resources by tag across multiple Regions and resource types in a single query. It is the quickest way to list every component tagged application=<value>.

others.A: CloudTrail records API activity and does not inventory resources by tag.
others.B: Querying each service in each Region with the CLI is slow and laborious.
others.C: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries log data, not resource tags.

tip: Find resources by tag across Regions = Tag Editor (or Resource Explorer).

why: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent, infrequent and archive instant access tiers based on changing access patterns. Its millisecond access tiers add no retrieval fees or latency, which suits variable, rapidly changing access to large objects.

others.B: Glacier Instant Retrieval has high retrieval fees and a 90-day minimum, so it is costly for frequent access.
others.C: S3 Standard is costlier when objects go unaccessed for long periods.
others.D: Standard-IA retrieval fees add up when access is unpredictable and sometimes heavy.

tip: Unknown or changing access patterns = Intelligent-Tiering.

why: AWS WAF is a managed web application firewall that attaches directly to an ALB. AWS managed rule groups block SQL injection and XSS with no servers to manage, reducing the customer's share of responsibility.

others.B: This option text is an artifact of the source data and is not a valid solution.
others.C: Shield Advanced focuses on DDoS, and WAF rules are what filter XSS or SQL injection.
others.D: A third-party firewall on EC2 increases servers to manage and patch.

tip: XSS or SQL injection = AWS WAF.

why: An AWS Glue crawler infers the CSV schema into the Data Catalog, and a Glue ETL job (which can be generated visually) converts CSV to Parquet and writes it to the target bucket. Glue is serverless with minimal code, so this is the least development effort.

others.A: An EMR cluster with a custom Spark app requires cluster management and coding.
others.C: AWS Batch with custom Bash conversion scripts requires significant development.
others.D: A Lambda function needs custom Parquet-conversion code and libraries, and it has runtime and memory limits.

tip: CSV to Parquet with least effort = Glue ETL.

why: Transferring 700 TB at 500 Mbps takes about 130 days, far beyond 1 month, so offline AWS Snowball devices are required. A Lifecycle rule to S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest storage for rarely accessed 7-year retention.

others.B: A VPN still uses the same 500 Mbps link, which is too slow for 700 TB in a month.
others.C: A 500 Mbps Direct Connect is equally too slow and adds cost and lead time.
others.D: DataSync over 500 Mbps cannot move 700 TB in a month, and Glacier Flexible Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive.

tip: Calculate transfer time: 1 Gbps moves about 10 TB per day; too slow means Snowball.

why: Turning on default bucket encryption covers all future uploads (S3 now encrypts new objects with SSE-S3 by default anyway). S3 Inventory identifies the unencrypted existing objects, and an S3 Batch Operations copy job re-encrypts millions of objects in place with minimal effort.

others.A: Downloading and re-uploading millions of objects to a new bucket is slow and laborious, and the CloudFront origin would need changing.
others.C: Changing default encryption and enabling versioning does not encrypt objects that already exist.
others.D: Modifying millions of objects one by one in the console is impractical.

tip: Bulk action on existing S3 objects = S3 Inventory + Batch Operations.

why: Deploying the required infrastructure in a second Region (pilot light or warm standby) with a cross-Region Aurora Replica keeps data nearly current. A Route 53 active-passive failover record switches traffic only when the primary fails, which fits the 30-minute RTO and RPO and the requirement that the standby does not serve traffic normally.

others.B: Active-active sends production traffic to the second Region, which the requirement says is not needed.
others.C: Active-active is unnecessary, and restoring from the latest snapshot risks more data loss and time.
others.D: Building infrastructure from backups at failover time risks exceeding 30 minutes, and Aurora does not support a second writable primary in another Region this way.

tip: Standby that does not take traffic = active-passive (failover) routing.

why: Security groups are stateful, so an inbound rule for TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 is enough (the default SG does not allow it). Network ACLs are stateless, so they need inbound 443 plus outbound ephemeral ports (1024-65535, or 32768-65535 for Linux) for the return traffic.

others.B: An outbound rule to a destination does not allow inbound HTTPS connections, and SG return traffic is automatic.
others.C: Allowing only inbound 443 on the stateless NACL blocks response traffic.
others.D: Responses go to client ephemeral ports, not port 443, so outbound 443 does not permit return traffic.

tip: SG stateful (inbound rule only); NACL stateless (allow ephemeral ports outbound).

why: The workload is memory-bound, so memory-optimized R5 instances fit, and updating the CloudFormation template keeps infrastructure as code. EC2 does not publish memory metrics natively, so installing the CloudWatch agent is required to collect memory and custom latency metrics for capacity planning.

others.A: Burstable T3 instances are not suited to sustained memory-heavy work, and console changes cause drift from CloudFormation.
others.B: Manual capacity changes are not operationally efficient, and scaling out a stateful app does not fix memory pressure.
others.C: CloudWatch has no built-in EC2 memory metrics; the agent is required.

tip: Memory metrics on EC2 = CloudWatch agent.

why: AWS Lambda bills only per request and duration with no idle cost, which is ideal when hours pass without traffic. It starts within milliseconds to seconds, meeting the 'within a few seconds' processing target at the lowest cost.

others.A: Glue jobs are for ETL and have startup times and minimum billing that are unsuitable for per-request API work.
others.C: An EKS cluster has control plane and node costs even while idle.
others.D: ECS on EC2 requires instances that cost money even when idle.

tip: Sporadic, short tasks at lowest cost = Lambda.

why: Amazon S3 is the cheapest durable storage for 7-year log retention, and lifecycle tiering can reduce cost further. Many clients or tools can read all objects concurrently through the API, and analytics tools such as Athena integrate with it directly.

others.A: EBS volumes are attached to one instance (Multi-AZ sharing is limited) and cost more per GB.
others.B: EFS supports concurrent access but costs much more than S3 for long-term retention.
others.C: Instance store is ephemeral and loses data when the instance stops.

tip: Long-term, cheap, concurrently accessible = S3.

why: A cross-account IAM role in the company's account with a trust policy for the vendor's account or role lets the vendor's tool assume it via STS for temporary credentials. Attached policies give least-privilege access, and an external ID is recommended for third parties.

others.B: An IAM user with long-term credentials for a third party is less secure and against best practice.
others.C: IAM groups can contain only users from the same account.
others.D: There is no 'AWS account' identity provider type; IdPs are for SAML or OIDC federation.

tip: Third-party or cross-account access = IAM role + trust policy (+ external ID).

why: Giving the pod an IAM role (IRSA or EKS Pod Identity) provides temporary credentials scoped to that pod. A gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB keeps traffic from the private subnets on the AWS network without internet access.

others.B: This option has no text in the source and is not a valid solution.
others.C: NACL changes alone do not create a private path to DynamoDB, and without an endpoint traffic would go via the internet.
others.E: Embedding access keys in code is insecure and against best practice.

tip: Pod permissions = IRSA or Pod Identity; private DynamoDB access = gateway endpoint.

why: A Route 53 multivalue answer policy returns up to eight healthy records chosen randomly, spreading traffic across all running instances with health checks. Four instances split two and two across two AZs remain fault tolerant if one AZ is lost.

others.A: Failover routing sends traffic to a primary and uses the secondary only on failure, so it does not reach all instances.
others.B: Weighted routing distributes by assigned weights rather than randomly across all healthy instances.
others.D: An uneven three-instance layout loses two-thirds of capacity if the larger AZ fails.

tip: Random distribution across healthy IPs = multivalue answer routing.

why: Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed, auto-scaling ingestion service that delivers directly into Amazon Redshift (staging through S3). Redshift supports petabyte-scale SQL analytics on existing and new data, so the combination has the least operational overhead.

others.A: Kinesis Data Streams cannot deliver to S3 by itself (it needs consumers or Firehose), and no SQL query layer is provided.
others.C: S3 plus Lambda provides no SQL analytics capability.
others.D: A custom EC2 ingestion service and RDS have high overhead and RDS does not scale to petabytes.

tip: Streaming into Redshift, S3 or OpenSearch with no code = Firehose.

why: API Gateway scales to accept requests from millions of devices without servers, Kinesis Data Streams buffers the data, and Firehose delivers it to S3. AWS Glue then transforms the raw data serverlessly, giving high scalability with minimal operations.

others.B: Route 53 routing across EC2 instances still requires managing and scaling servers.
others.C: Adding EC2 instances manually increases operational overhead.
others.D: EC2 consumers for SQS still require managing instances.

tip: Massive device ingestion serverless = API Gateway + Kinesis + Firehose.

why: With versioning enabled, the current-version expiration action only adds delete markers and keeps the old versions. Adding a NoncurrentVersionExpiration rule (and expired delete marker cleanup) to the Lifecycle policy actually removes them at no extra cost.

others.A: CloudTrail trails have no setting to expire objects in S3.
others.C: A custom Lambda function costs more and is more effort than a native Lifecycle rule.
others.D: Object ownership does not affect lifecycle deletion of noncurrent versions.

tip: Versioned bucket still growing = expire noncurrent versions.

why: Writing incoming data to SQS absorbs traffic spikes durably so no data is lost. Lambda consumers with a limited batch size and maximum concurrency write to RDS at a controlled rate, minimizing database connections.

others.A: A larger instance may help but does not cap connections or guarantee no data loss during spikes.
others.B: Multi-AZ standbys are not writable, so writing to all instances is not possible.
others.D: SNS pushes immediately to Lambda with no buffering or throttling, so the database is still overwhelmed.

tip: Smooth write spikes to a database = SQS buffer.

why: Aurora Serverless (v2) for MySQL scales compute capacity up and down automatically. It keeps MySQL compatibility, so no engine change is needed, and Aurora's six-way replicated storage gives better performance and durability with minimal operations effort.

others.B: Aurora PostgreSQL would require migrating from MySQL to a different engine.
others.C: One larger self-managed instance still requires manual scaling and replication.
others.D: Databases cannot simply be auto scaled in an EC2 Auto Scaling group, and replication remains manual.

tip: Auto-scaling MySQL compute with minimal effort = Aurora Serverless MySQL.

why: NAT gateways are managed, scale automatically up to 100 Gbps, and are redundant within an AZ. Placing one in each of two AZs, with each AZ's private subnets routed to their local gateway, provides high availability and fault tolerance.

others.A: Two NAT gateways in the same AZ fail together if that AZ fails.
others.B: NAT instances behind an NLB are self-managed and do not work as an Auto Scaling NAT solution.
others.D: Spot NAT instances can be interrupted and are still self-managed.

tip: NAT HA = one NAT gateway per AZ.

why: The intended keyed answer B is a VPC peering connection between VPC A and VPC B. It lets the application reach the database over private IPs on the AWS network, with security groups allowing only the application, and nothing is exposed publicly.

others.A: This option text is missing in the source; it was a DB security group allowing the app server's public IP, which forces traffic over public IPs.
others.C: Making the database publicly accessible exposes it to the internet, which is the least secure option.
others.D: A proxy EC2 instance with an Elastic IP adds a public-facing component and management overhead.

tip: Private access between two VPCs = VPC peering (or Transit Gateway at scale).
flag: Source data is garbled: the keyed option B text shows 'Proxy all requests through the new EC2 instance' (a fragment of option D), but the intended correct answer is VPC peering between VPC A and VPC B.

why: VPC Flow Logs published to CloudWatch Logs capture accepted connections on ports 22 and 3389. A metric filter counts those events, and a CloudWatch alarm with an SNS notification alerts the operations team when RDP or SSH access occurs.

others.A: CloudWatch Application Insights monitors application health problems, not network RDP or SSH connections.
others.B: An SSM instance profile enables Systems Manager management but does not by itself notify anyone of RDP or SSH sessions.
others.D: Instance state-change events report starts and stops, not login connections.

tip: Detect traffic on specific ports = VPC Flow Logs + metric filter + alarm.

why: Securing the root user starts with a strong, unique password and MFA, which AWS strongly recommends (and now enforces for many account types). These two actions directly protect root sign-in.

others.C: Root access keys should not exist at all; delete them rather than store them.
others.D: The root user cannot be added to IAM groups.
others.E: IAM policies cannot be attached to the root user, which always has full access.

tip: Root user: strong password, MFA, no access keys, use rarely.

why: AWS KMS keys encrypt EBS volumes and Aurora storage at rest. An ACM certificate on the ALB's HTTPS listener encrypts data in transit, which is the standard AWS-native pattern.

others.A: The roles are reversed: KMS does not issue certificates, and ACM does not encrypt storage.
others.B: There is no single account-wide encryption switch, and using the root account for daily tasks is bad practice.
others.D: BitLocker does not encrypt Aurora storage, and KMS keys cannot be attached to an ALB for TLS.

tip: At rest = KMS; in transit on ALB or CloudFront = ACM certificate.

why: Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL is heterogeneous, so AWS SCT converts the schema. DMS with full load plus CDC on all tables keeps both databases in sync during the month-by-month cutovers, and a memory-optimized replication instance suits heavy read and write CDC workloads.

others.A: DataSync moves files, not database contents, and CDC alone lacks the initial load.
others.B: DataSync cannot migrate a live database, and the schema conversion step is missing.
others.D: Selecting only the largest tables leaves other tables unsynced, and memory-optimized instances are recommended for CDC.

tip: Heterogeneous migration = SCT + DMS; stay in sync = full load + CDC.

why: Elastic Beanstalk Multi-AZ, load-balanced environments run the existing front-end and application code with auto scaling and high availability and little change. RDS Multi-AZ provides an HA MySQL database, and S3 is the scalable store for images.

others.A: Rewriting to S3, Lambda and DynamoDB requires major application changes.
others.B: Read replicas do not provide automatic failover, and images do not belong in the database.
others.C: A single memory-optimized database instance is not highly available, and storing images in the database is a poor design.

tip: Least change + HA = Beanstalk Multi-AZ + RDS Multi-AZ + S3 for media.

why: The intended keyed answer A is a VPC peering connection between VPC-A and VPC-B across accounts. Peering is not a single physical gateway, so it has no single point of failure and no bandwidth bottleneck, and traffic stays private on the AWS network.

others.B: This option has no text in the source and is not a valid solution.
others.C: A virtual private gateway is for VPN or Direct Connect to on-premises networks, and VPN tunnels carry bandwidth limits.
others.D: A private VIF is a Direct Connect construct for on-premises connectivity and does not attach to an EC2 instance.

tip: VPC peering has no SPOF and no bandwidth bottleneck.
flag: Source data is garbled: option A text reads 'Correct Answer: A' instead of the intended 'Set up a VPC peering connection between VPC-A and VPC-B'; the keyed letter is right.

why: AWS Budgets lets you create a monthly cost budget per account scoped to EC2. Alerts are sent through email or SNS when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold, and the first budgets are free, making it the most cost-effective option.

others.A: Cost Explorer reports do not send threshold alerts via SES.
others.B: Cost Explorer reports still have no SES threshold notification capability.
others.D: CUR with Athena and scheduled queries is complex and costs more for a simple threshold alert.

tip: Alert when spend or usage exceeds a threshold = AWS Budgets.

why: API Gateway REST APIs provide an HTTPS endpoint with IAM (SigV4) authorization integrated with Lambda. This is the classic answer, offering throttling, stages and other API management features.

others.B: Lambda function URLs also provide HTTPS with AWS_IAM auth and are simpler, but the keyed answer favours API Gateway.
others.C: Writing custom IAM authentication logic in Lambda@Edge is complex, and Lambda@Edge has runtime restrictions.
others.D: CloudFront Functions support only JavaScript, cannot run Go, and have no AWS_IAM auth type.

tip: Function URLs = simplest HTTPS endpoint for one function; API Gateway = full API management.
flag: A Lambda function URL with AuthType AWS_IAM (B) gives an HTTPS endpoint with IAM auth for a single function with less setup, so B is arguably the most operationally efficient answer.

why: Hosting the visualization tool in the same Region as the warehouse means the 50 MB query results never leave AWS (intra-Region transfer). Only the 500 KB webpages egress, and over Direct Connect, whose data transfer out rates are lower than internet rates.

others.A: 50 MB results egress over the internet at the highest rates.
others.B: Internet egress for webpages costs more than egress over Direct Connect.
others.C: The 50 MB result sets still egress (although at DX rates), which is much more data than 500 KB pages.

tip: Minimize egress: keep heavy traffic inside AWS and send only small results out via DX.

why: RDS for PostgreSQL with a cross-Region read replica keeps a continuously replicated, online copy of the data in another Region. It is managed and can be promoted, giving multi-Region availability with low operational overhead.

others.A: A self-managed PostgreSQL cluster on EC2 has high operational overhead.
others.B: Multi-AZ provides availability within a single Region only.
others.D: Snapshot copies are not online and available at all times.

tip: Data in multiple Regions = cross-Region read replica (or Aurora Global Database).

why: A Route 53 multivalue answer routing policy returns multiple IP addresses (up to eight healthy records per response) and uses health checks to return only healthy instances.

others.A: Simple routing returns all values but cannot use health checks to omit unhealthy instances.
others.B: Latency routing returns the single record with the lowest latency.
others.D: Geolocation routing returns records based on user location, not all healthy IPs.

tip: Multiple healthy IPs in DNS answers = multivalue answer.

why: An S3 File Gateway deployed as a VM at each clinic presents the S3 bucket as an NFS or SMB file share to on-premises file-based applications. It caches data locally for low-latency access while S3 remains the source of truth.

others.B: DataSync copies data on a schedule and does not provide ongoing low-latency file access with S3 permissions.
others.C: Volume Gateway presents block iSCSI volumes, not file access to S3 objects.
others.D: EFS is not designed to be mounted directly by remote clinics across the country, and the data is in S3.

tip: On-premises file access to S3 = S3 File Gateway.

why: Separating the database into Aurora with a replica in another AZ provides database HA through automatic failover. An AMI-based Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind an ALB makes the web tier both highly available and scalable.

others.A: Everything stays in one AZ, and manually launched instances do not scale.
others.B: A replica and instances all in one AZ are not highly available, and there is no Auto Scaling.
others.D: A self-managed database on a single EC2 instance is a single point of failure.

tip: HA + scale = multi-AZ Auto Scaling group + ALB + multi-AZ database.

why: Reducing the development Auto Scaling group's maximum capacity stops dev from scaling out to costly levels while keeping the setup the same. Production is unaffected and can still scale for high traffic.

others.A: Targets are managed by the Auto Scaling group, so manually setting one target is not durable, and the stated minimum is two instances.
others.B: Changing the load balancing algorithm does not reduce cost.
others.C: Shrinking production instances risks performance during high-traffic periods.

tip: Dev cost control = cap Auto Scaling capacity or use smaller or fewer instances only in dev.

why: An internet-facing ALB must be placed in public subnets (with a route to an internet gateway) in each AZ. It can then forward traffic to targets in private subnets, so creating public subnets and associating them with the ALB fixes the problem.

others.A: An NLB has the same subnet requirement, and NAT gateways only handle outbound traffic, not inbound.
others.B: Routes between subnets in a VPC already exist through the local route.
others.C: Making the instance subnets public defeats the private design and does not fix the ALB subnet placement.

tip: Internet-facing ALB = public subnets; targets can stay private.

why: RDS read replicas require automated backups (backup retention greater than 0) on the source. AWS also recommends letting long-running transactions finish before creating a replica, because replica creation starts from a snapshot and long transactions can delay or break replication.

others.A: Binary logging is managed by RDS automatically once backups are enabled; there is no separate setting to turn on.
others.B: Failover priority (tiers) applies to Aurora replicas, not RDS for MySQL source instances.
others.D: Global tables are a DynamoDB feature.

tip: RDS read replica prerequisite = automated backups enabled.

why: Putting job requests into SQS ensures none are lost while instances are busy. An EC2 Auto Scaling group scaling on queue depth (or backlog per instance) adds workers with user load and improves throughput.

others.A: A copied instance behind an ALB is a fixed capacity increase with no automatic scaling, and requests can still be dropped.
others.B: An S3 endpoint changes network routing, not CPU saturation.
others.C: Vertical scaling needs downtime and does not scale with user load.

tip: Jobs dropped under load = SQS + Auto Scaling on queue depth.

why: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed native Windows file system accessible over SMB. It suits shared storage for a media application in the cloud.

others.A: Volume Gateway exposes iSCSI block volumes, not SMB file shares, and is for hybrid use.
others.B: Tape Gateway provides a virtual tape library for backup, not shared SMB storage.
others.C: A self-managed Windows file server on EC2 is not fully managed.

tip: Managed SMB = FSx for Windows (or FSx for NetApp ONTAP).

why: Delivering VPC Flow Logs to S3 is low cost, and a Lifecycle rule moves logs to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days, matching frequent access for 90 days and intermittent access afterwards.

others.A: Expiring the log group after 90 days deletes the logs, losing the intermittent access afterwards.
others.B: Kinesis Data Streams is not a Flow Logs destination and is not suited to long-term storage.
others.C: CloudTrail records API calls and is not a VPC Flow Logs destination.

tip: Flow Logs destinations: CloudWatch Logs, S3, Firehose.

why: A NAT gateway in a public subnet, with the private subnet's default route (0.0.0.0/0) pointing to it, lets the instance make outbound connections for updates. Unsolicited inbound traffic is still blocked.

others.A: An internet gateway alone does not give a private instance without a public IP outbound access, and the option is incomplete.
others.C: A NAT instance must be in a public subnet, and the private route should point to the NAT, not the internet gateway.
others.D: An internet gateway alone does not provide outbound access for private instances, and the option is incomplete.

tip: Private subnet outbound internet = NAT gateway in a public subnet.

why: Amazon EFS is a managed NFS file system that many EC2 instances can mount simultaneously. It grows elastically and stores data redundantly across multiple AZs.

others.B: EBS volumes attach to a single instance (Multi-Attach is limited) and are AZ-scoped.
others.C: Glacier Deep Archive is archival with hours-long retrieval, not live shared access.
others.D: AWS Backup is a backup service, not primary shared storage.

tip: Shared, growing Linux file storage across instances = EFS.

why: The policy JSON images are missing from the source. In the original question, the combined policies allow ec2 actions including TerminateInstances (deleting EC2 instances), while an explicit Deny or the absence of an Allow prevents the other actions.

others.A: The IAM delete-user action is not allowed by the policies (explicitly denied or not granted).
others.B: Directory Service deletion actions are denied or not granted by the policies.
others.D: CloudWatch Logs delete actions are denied or not granted by the policies.

tip: IAM evaluation: explicit Deny beats Allow; no Allow means implicit deny.

why: Storing the order once and sending its order number to an SQS FIFO queue provides exactly-once processing and message deduplication. The payment service processes each order once and deletes the message, preventing duplicate orders on resubmission.

others.A: Firehose is a delivery stream to destinations, not a queue that consumers retrieve from, and it does not deduplicate.
others.B: CloudTrail logs AWS API calls and does not trigger on application request paths.
others.C: SNS is push-based and cannot be polled, and it offers no deduplication here.

tip: Prevent duplicates = SQS FIFO deduplication (or idempotency keys).

why: Versioning keeps every version of each document, so modifications and uploads create new versions and deletes become recoverable delete markers. MFA Delete requires MFA to permanently delete versions or change the versioning state, preventing accidental deletion.

others.A: A read-only ACL would stop users from uploading modified documents.
others.C: IAM policies attach to identities rather than buckets, and a policy alone does not keep versions.
others.E: KMS encryption protects confidentiality but does nothing against deletion.

tip: Prevent accidental deletion = Versioning + MFA Delete (or Object Lock).
